ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, the intersection of the line $y=-x+m$ with $y=nx+4n\ (n\ne 0)$ has an abscissa of $-2$. How many integer solutions are there for the inequality $-x+m>nx+4n>0$ with respect to $x$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text: \textbf{Solution}: When $y=0$, for $y=nx+4n\ (n\ne 0)$, then $x=-4$. Therefore, the solution set for $nx+4n>0$ is $x>-4$. Since the $x$-coordinate of the intersection point between $y=-x+m$ and $y=nx+4n\ (n\ne 0)$ is $-2$, observing the graph shows that the solution set for $-x+m>nx+4n$ is $x<-2$. Hence, the solution set for $-x+m>nx+4n>0$ is $-4<x<-2$. Since $x$ is an integer, it follows that $x=\boxed{-3}$.

Since the $x$-coordinate of the intersection point between $y=-x+m$ and $y=nx+4n\ (n\ne 0)$ is $-2$, observing the graph shows that the solution set for $-x+m>nx+4n$ is $x<-2$. Hence, the solution set for $-x+m>nx+4n>0$ is $-4<x<-2$. Since $x$ is an integer, it follows that $x=\boxed{-3}$.

ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there are two straight lines, one labeled y=-x+m, showing a descending trend from upper left to lower right; the other labeled y=nx+4n, showing an ascending trend from lower left to upper right. The two straight lines intersect, and a dashed perpendicular line is drawn from the intersection point to the x-axis, with the foot labeled x=-2. Reasoning: Need to solve the compound inequality -x+m>nx+4n>0. First look at nx+4n>0: from y=nx+4n=n(x+4), when y=0, x=-4; also because this straight line in the figure slopes upward to the right, that is n>0, so nx+4n>0 corresponds to x>-4. Then look at -x+m>nx+4n: from the image it can be seen that to the left of the intersection of the two lines x=-2, the descending straight line y=-x+m is above the ascending straight line y=nx+4n, so -x+m>nx+4n corresponds to x<-2. Combining the two conditions gives -4<x<-2. The only integer in this open interval is x=-3, therefore the number of integer solutions is 1.
